summary:
Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which applies in full; no regional deviation from that framework has been identified. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025) states that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The 2013 "gay propaganda" law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, rising to up to four years' imprisonment on repeat offence; since the 2023 extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries two to six years and organising six to ten years' imprisonment. The note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. It states that foreigners found guilty of violating the "propaganda" law may be arrested and detained for up to 15 days and then deported, that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and it advises against all travel to Russia.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of that date, comprising about 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night (The Guardian, 17 January 2024).

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented: BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement wave is national rather than regional: the figures compiled by Human Rights Watch, Meduza and the UK Home Office describe country-wide totals, and no separate statistics for Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra were located in the sources. A visitor should therefore expect Moscow-pattern outcomes here, since the operative statutes are federal.

The regime is comparatively unusual in that same-sex sexual activity itself is not criminalised while expression about it is, and gender transition is simultaneously prohibited in law and healthcare. The practical exposure for a transgender visitor rests less on private conduct than on visible symbols, documents and statements: displaying the rainbow flag is treated as a crime, and expression "justifying" gender transition falls within the propaganda offence.

The designated extremist status converts relatively minor conduct into escalating exposure. The administrative route under article 20.3 produced 98 convictions in roughly eighteen months, while the criminal route under article 282.2 carries up to twelve years, and repeat propaganda offences move from fines and short detention to four years' imprisonment.

The autonomous republic of Chechnya is cited in the UK Home Office note as part of the same country-wide finding on particular social group membership, illustrating that regional variation inside Russia has not displaced the national assessment.

Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year, so gender-affirming medical care is unavailable through lawful channels.

Same-sex marriage is banned for residents, while same-sex sexual activity is not itself a criminal offence. Residents face administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days for propaganda-type expression, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on repeat offence, and since the 2023 extremist designation participation carries two to six years and organising six to ten years' imprisonment.

The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that the state is able but unwilling to protect openly LGBT+ people from societal discrimination that may amount to persecution. Russian citizens who leave the country may be assessed as members of a particular social group under the refugee convention for UK asylum purposes. Residents displaying banned symbols are exposed under article 20.3, which accounted for 81 convictions across 98 administrative cases between January 2024 and June 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement data specific to Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra was found in the source inventory. Whether convictions, raids or administrative cases under articles 20.3 and 282.2 have occurred within the okrug is unresolved and not sourced here.

The sources do not state whether law-enforcement practice in the okrug diverges in any way from the national pattern, and no regional deviation was identified. This is an absence of sourced evidence, not a finding that no divergence exists.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian took place near Novosibirsk, not in this okrug; it is cited as evidence of documented physical coercion against transgender people nationally, and its occurrence locally is unresolved.

Local conditions for transgender residents outside major urban centres, including access to documentation services, private medical care and hate-crime victim support in the okrug, are not covered by the sources reviewed.
